Apple may unveil the iPad 3 later this fall, according to rumors from TechCrunch and Daring Fireball. This would come shortly after the iPad 2, surprising many given Apple's usual product development cycles. The plan is reportedly to release one iPad iteration in the next few weeks, followed by a new version in the fall. While details are scarce, the iPad 3 could feature a high-resolution display similar to the iPhone 4, and a smaller form factor. Apple's history of not resting on its laurels suggests they aim to stay ahead in the tablet market.

On World AIDS Day, a medical breakthrough offers hope: An HIV-positive man, known as the "Berlin Patient," has been declared cured after receiving a stem cell transplant. Doctors, publishing in the journal Blood, suggest his case points to a potential permanent cure through genetically engineered stem cells. This breakthrough, alongside other recent findings, could significantly impact the lives of the 33 million people living with HIV worldwide.

Charlie Sheen and Warner Bros. have settled their legal dispute over "Two and a Half Men," with both parties agreeing to dismiss their lawsuits. A Warner Bros. representative stated that the resolution was satisfactory to all involved. Sheen is set to receive approximately $100 million in profits from the show's syndication over the next seven years, primarily for work he has already performed and profits he has already earned.

A destructive invasive rodent called the nutria, which can weigh up to 20 pounds and measure 2 feet 6 inches long, including a 12-inch tail, has been spotted in Stanislaus, Merced, and Fresno counties, raising concerns about potential damage to infrastructure and agriculture. These rodents can consume 25% of their body weight in vegetation daily and can produce up to 200 offspring annually, making eradication efforts crucial. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife has set traps and deployed trail cameras to monitor the situation and has called for public assistance in reporting sightings. Nutria, originally introduced to California for fur in 1899, were thought to be eradicated by 1978 but may have remained undetected, reemerging only recently. Parental happiness varies significantly across 22 countries, with the U.S. showing the largest gap between parents and non-parents. A study by Jennifer Glass, Robin Simon, and Matthew Andersson found that social policies supporting the combination of work and family life can eliminate the happiness penalty for parents. Countries with better family support policies, such as paid leave, sick and vacation days, and affordable childcare, reported no happiness gap or even higher happiness among parents compared to non-parents. These policies benefit everyone, not just parents, by improving overall well-being. The researchers suggest that implementing such policies could help increase fertility rates and improve public health.

A 17-year-old student, the son of a police detective, opened fire at Millard South High School in Omaha, Nebraska, on Wednesday, fatally wounding the assistant principal and forcing students to take cover in the kitchen. The shooter, who had attended the school for no more than two months, also wounded the principal before fleeing and fatally shooting himself in his car about a mile away. Assistant Principal Vicki Kaspar died at a hospital, while Principal Curtis Case was listed in stable condition. The shooter's final Facebook post expressed unhappiness with his new school and apologized for the lives he ruined. Friends described him as energetic and outgoing, but authorities are investigating what may have led to the violence. The school was immediately locked down, and students were eventually released in groups.

The Leonid meteor shower is set to peak this weekend, offering a chance to see up to 15 meteors per hour. This annual event, occurring in mid-November, will be visible from late Saturday night into Sunday morning. However, the waxing gibbous moon will compete for visibility, so the best viewing times are after the moon sets and before dawn. To maximize your chances of seeing meteors, find a location away from city lights and give your eyes time to adjust to the darkness. NASA suggests using a sleeping bag, blanket, or lawn chair for comfort. The meteors appear to originate from the constellation Leo, but the best view is away from this point. These meteors travel at 45 miles per second, creating bright trails and occasionally fireballs. An unarmed security guard at Las Vegas' Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino played a crucial role in stopping the deadliest mass shooting in modern American history. Jesus Campos, identified by the International Union, Security, Police and Fire Professionals of America, was the first to engage with gunman Stephen Paddock, getting shot in the process. Campos managed to direct police to Paddock's 32nd-floor suite and provided a hotel key to officers. Despite being shot in the leg, he continued to help clear rooms on the same floor before insisting on medical attention. Undersheriff Kevin McMahill praised Campos as an "absolute hero" who fired over 200 rounds at him when approaching. Paddock had set up a camera in the hallway to watch for authorities. The security guard's actions were crucial in locating and ending the massacre, which left 58 people dead and hundreds injured.

Parents of some of the Sandy Hook victims are set to sue Bushmaster, the manufacturer of the AR-15 used by Adam Lanza. They are working with a lawyer who represented Michael Jackson’s family in a wrongful death lawsuit and a lobbyist who worked for the Clinton administration. This legal action, to be announced on Monday, aims to hold Bushmaster accountable for the mass shooting, which killed 20 first-grade students and six educators. The parents have opened estates in their children’s names to pursue wrongful death claims, with the deadline for filing lawsuits approaching the second anniversary of the tragedy.

A South Carolina newlywed and nurse, Brittany Oswell, died after suffering an embolism and cardiac arrest during a flight from Honolulu to Dallas-Fort Worth with a connection in Dallas-Fort Worth to Columbia, South Carolina, on April 15, 2016. Her husband, Cory Oswell, and her parents, Christopher and Tina Starks, have filed a wrongful death lawsuit against American Airlines. According to the lawsuit, Brittany began feeling ill with dizziness and disorientation, and her speech slurred before she fainted. A doctor on the flight initially thought she was having a panic attack. Later, she collapsed, vomited, and defecated in the lavatory. The doctor urged an emergency landing but the crew did not divert the flight, citing about 90 minutes left until Dallas. Sharbat Gula, known as the "Afghan Girl" from a 1985 National Geographic cover photo, was arrested in Pakistan for allegedly possessing a fake national identification card, authorities said. The iconic green-eyed refugee, who gained fame after photographer Steve McCurry captured her image, was arrested in Peshawar following a two-year investigation. She could face up to 14 years in prison. Gula, who was about 12 years old when McCurry took her photo, became a symbol of the refugee plight and later returned to Afghanistan, where she was married and had three daughters. Pakistan has been cracking down on fake IDs, with over 60,000 fraudulent cards seized. The arrest highlights ongoing challenges for refugees in Pakistan, amid efforts to verify identities and pressure for Afghans to leave the country.

Taylor Swift filed a counter suit against David Mueller, a radio host who alleged he was wrongfully fired and banned from her concerts based on false accusations of groping her at a 2013 meet-and-greet. Mueller's lawsuit claimed he was assaulted by Swift's former employer, Eddie Haskell, but Swift's countersuit states Mueller was the actual perpetrator. The countersuit details that Mueller intentionally groped Swift's intimate area during a meet-and-greet, causing her to become upset and alert her security team. Swift demands a jury trial and plans to donate any winnings to organizations supporting women against sexual assault.

Kristen Wiig will return to host Saturday Night Live on May 11th, marking her first appearance since wrapping a seven-year stint on the show. Her hosting debut will feature musical guest Vampire Weekend. Ben Affleck will close out the 38th season on May 18th, with Kanye West as musical guest. Wiig's film career is thriving, with upcoming projects including Bridesmaids, Girl Most Likely, Despicable Me 2, Anchorman: The Legend Continues, and The Secret Life of Walter Mitty.

The Thomas fire, the largest recorded wildfire in California history, has been officially declared extinguished after burning over 440 square miles and destroying more than 1,000 buildings. The blaze, which began near Thomas Aquinas College in December 2017, raced through Ventura and Santa Barbara counties, killing two people, including a state firefighter. A massive downpour on January 9, 2018, triggered deadly mudslides, killing 21 people and leaving two missing in the Montecito community. The fire's cause remains under investigation, with lawsuits filed against Southern California Edison. Nearly six months after it started, crews are now repairing roads, trails, and fences damaged by the blaze and subsequent rainstorms. A new startup called OUYA is aiming to disrupt the console gaming market with an open Android-powered device priced at just $99. The company is launching a Kickstarter campaign to raise funds, with the goal of bringing the console to market by the first quarter of 2013. OUYA encourages developers to create games for its platform, with the requirement that at least a portion of the games must be free to try. The console features a touchpad controller designed by Yves Behar, and runs on a Tegra 3 processor. OUYA aims to bring innovation and experimentation back to console gaming, making it more accessible and affordable for developers and gamers alike.

Neil Armstrong, the first man to walk on the moon, has died at the age of 82. He commanded the Apollo 11 mission that landed on the moon on July 20, 1969, famously saying "That's one small step for (a) man, one giant leap for mankind." Armstrong was a quiet, modest engineer who preferred to focus on the team that helped him achieve his historic feat rather than his own accomplishments. Despite his fame, he largely stayed out of the public eye, rarely giving interviews and avoiding the spotlight. His family requested that people honor his modesty by remembering his example of service, accomplishment, and humility.

More than 24 million voter-registration records in the U.S. are inaccurate, out-of-date, or duplicates, according to a report by the Pew Center on the States. About one in eight voter registrations is affected, with nearly 2.8 million people registered in two or more states and perhaps 1.8 million registered voters who are deceased. Experts say this largely paper-based system is outdated, expensive, and error-prone, leading to wasted resources on mailings and extra ballots. Inaccurate voter lists also cost money and undermine voter confidence. Swing states, where voter registration efforts are more frequent, face particularly significant challenges. Solutions include creating multistate data centers to help election officials spot records that could be removed, though the motor voter law still requires voters to take affirmative action.

Bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) can remember each other's signature contact whistles—unique calls that function like names—for over two decades, according to a new study. This is the longest social memory ever recorded in a non-human animal. The research, conducted by Jason Bruck at the University of Chicago, involved collecting 71 whistles from 43 dolphins across six captive facilities. When played recordings of whistles from dolphins they had previously lived with, the animals often approached the speaker, showing recognition even after 20.5 years of separation. This finding suggests that dolphins have long-term social recognition, which could help them navigate their complex social groups. The study, published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B, indicates that dolphins' cognitive abilities are on par with those of humans, chimpanzees, and elephants.

The first nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System via cellphones is set for Wednesday at 2:18 p.m. ET, with President Donald Trump not personally triggering the alert, a Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) official said. The test, aimed at ensuring the system works for a national emergency, will send a "Presidential Alert" message to nearly 225 million U.S. cellphones, with a loud tone and special vibration. The message will read: "THIS IS A TEST of the National Wireless Emergency Alert System. No action is needed." The test follows a law signed by President Obama in 2016 requiring FEMA to create a system for presidential alerts. Government officials estimate that while the alert will reach around 75% of all phones, those on a call lasting 30 minutes may not receive it. The test aims to address issues from a previous regional test, with some devices not receiving alerts.

A new study suggests that inheriting Alzheimer's disease from a mother may be more detrimental than from a father, as it leads to a greater loss of gray matter in the brain, particularly in areas involved in memory. Researchers from the University of Kansas School of Medicine examined 21 cognitively intact adult children (ages 63 to 83) with a family history of Alzheimer's and compared their brain scans to those of 32 healthy adults without such a history. While both groups showed similar levels of education and cognitive performance, those with a maternal history of Alzheimer's experienced more significant brain atrophy, especially in the left precuneus and left parahippocampal gyrus. The study, published in the March 1 edition of Neurology, indicates that the disease's inheritance pattern may be linked to mitochondrial DNA, which is only passed down from mothers and may affect glucose metabolism in the brain.

Democratic Rep. Kyrsten Sinema holds a narrow lead over Republican Rep. Martha McSally in Arizona's uncalled Senate race, with Sinema leading by 9,610 votes as of Thursday evening. Most of the remaining ballots are from Maricopa County, which includes Sinema's congressional district. Both campaigns are confident in their candidate's victory once all votes are counted. The race is one of the most expensive in the country, with nearly $30 million spent by both parties. Arizona is one of three remaining states without a declared winner, alongside Florida and Mississippi. The outcome could affect the Republican majority in the Senate, as Democrats need to defend 22 seats compared to just 12 for Republicans in the 2020 elections.

Shadow, a declawed male domestic grey shorthair cat, was adopted from the Pennsylvania Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals at 12 weeks old. Due to a severe anaphylactic allergy to cats, his owner had to relinquish him. He is neutered, up to date on vaccinations, and on a special diet to help him relax. Shadow enjoys sleeping by the fire and being close to his owners, following them around and sitting by their feet or laps. He avoids being petted near his tail. He came to VIPP on November 11, 2015.

A new guideline from the American Academy of Pediatrics discourages any screen time for babies under two years old, citing potential links to slower language development. Doctors warn that passive screen viewing, whether on a smartphone, computer, or television, can negatively impact a child's language skills. Pediatrician Ari Brown calls this "secondhand TV," noting that when the TV is on, parents tend to talk less to their children. The guideline also emphasizes the negative effects of parents' own screen-watching habits on their children. While interactive play such as video games is not included in the restrictions, the AAP recommends no more than two hours of screen time per day for children over two years old. The update to the guidelines comes amid concerns over the $200 million annual market for baby DVDs, many of which make educational claims despite a lack of proven educational benefits. The AAP advises parents to prioritize unstructured playtime for their children's developing brains.

Beauty queen Kim Kardashian-West, known for her heavily contoured look, is now advocating for a more natural, nontouring aesthetic. At the Vogue Festival in association with Harrods, she revealed she's moving away from heavy contouring, preferring to wear less makeup and focusing on strobing. Kim, who gave birth to her second child, Saint, without makeup, also shared her new minimalist makeup routine, including products from Charlotte Tilbury and her own line. She credits her mother's makeup collection and her father's decision to send her and her sister to makeup school for her love of beauty. Despite this shift, the event ended with a perfect selfie, highlighting the enduring appeal of a well-executed makeup look.

Diet Coke's "You're on" campaign, introduced three months ago, is being replaced after facing mockery on social media. The new campaign, "Just for the taste of it," which launched in 1982, will debut with print and TV ads. The "You're on" ads, intended to highlight the drink as a pick-me-up for young strivers, have been criticized for potentially referencing drug use. While Coca-Cola denies any such intent, the campaign's sudden end reflects the pressure from public perception. The new ads focus on the taste and sugar-free benefits of Diet Coke, aiming to resonate with core loyal followers. The shift comes as Diet Coke faces declining sales, part of a broader trend in the diet soda category.

Michelle Williams, 37, has married indie musician Phil Elverum, 40, in a private ceremony with close friends and their daughters present, marking a new chapter in her life. Williams, known for her private nature, reveals this in a Vanity Fair profile, highlighting the "very sacred and special" nature of their relationship. They met through mutual friends, and Elverum has also experienced loss, having lost his wife, Geneviève Castrée, to cancer. Williams, who has coped with her own grief since Heath Ledger's death in 2008, finds in Elverum a sense of "radical acceptance" and freedom. Her openness about this relationship, and her recent advocacy for gender pay equity in Hollywood, aims to inspire others facing similar struggles.

President Donald Trump took steps to advance construction of the Keystone XL and Dakota Access oil pipelines, while demanding a renegotiation for better deals for the U.S. government. Trump stopped short of green-lighting construction on either pipeline but put a deadline on the government’s review of TransCanada Corp.’s proposed Keystone XL. He also announced policies to encourage the use of American-made products in U.S. pipeline projects and to curtail federal environmental reviews for major infrastructure projects. Trump said, "If we’re going to build pipelines in the United States, the pipes should be made in the United States." The moves are a major departure from the Obama administration, which rejected the Keystone proposal in 2015 and has kept Dakota Access blocked since September. Environmentalists now face an executive branch that’s less sympathetic to their efforts, while the oil industry sees more freedom to expand infrastructure.

One of President Trump’s earliest decisions regarding the fight against the Islamic State was made by Michael Flynn weeks before he was fired, and it aligned with Turkey’s interests, which he had been paid over $500,000 to represent. Flynn, who was Trump’s national security adviser, delayed a military operation to retake Raqqa, the Islamic State’s de facto capital, with Syrian Kurdish forces, despite the Pentagon’s plan to use them as its most effective military partners. This decision was made 10 days before Trump’s inauguration, and it was consistent with Turkey’s opposition to partnering with the Kurdish forces. Flynn’s actions raise questions about his role in other key decisions during his brief tenure, and they highlight the potential legal issues he faces. Members of Congress are citing his intervention as a serious compromise, potentially involving treason, given his undisclosed foreign agent status. Despite the Trump administration’s attempts to downplay the situation, it is becoming clear that Flynn was repeatedly warned about his foreign involvement

BP's $20 billion oil spill compensation fund is nearly depleted, with only $300 million left, and the deadline for economic loss claims from Gulf coast businesses is not until April next year. BP shares fell 3.4% after the company increased its overall provision for the Gulf of Mexico oil spill to $42.4 billion. Bob Dudley, BP's chief executive, stated that plaintiffs' lawyers are the biggest beneficiaries, as they continue to submit large claims and ensure their own firms receive compensation. Dudley criticized the U.S. Department of Justice's interpretation of the agreement that allowed people to claim compensation, arguing that it was being misinterpreted and harming American businesses. He suggested that the plaintiffs' lawyers are motivated by their business model, which requires them to constantly seek out cases that can be turned into mass torts to extract billions from companies.

A Navy commander who faked his death to end an affair with a mistress has been relieved of his duties as the commanding officer of the USS Pittsburgh, just a week after taking command. The woman, who met the commander through an online dating service, became pregnant and lost the baby due to complications. Navy documents show the commander sent his mistress a fake email from a man named "Bob" in July, claiming he had died unexpectedly. The commander, currently assigned to a submarine group in Groton, has received a letter of reprimand for adultery and other military violations, and paperwork has been filed to remove him from the Navy. The woman, who was accompanied by a friend when she visited the commander's former residence in Virginia, was surprised to learn he was still alive and had moved to Connecticut.

Sen. Lindsey Graham and former Arkansas governor Mike Huckabee joined other Republicans in declaring their 2016 presidential intentions this week. On NBC's "Meet the Press," Graham announced he has set up a committee to explore a potential bid. On ABC's "This Week," Huckabee said he may declare his intentions later in spring, contingent on his campaign's fundraising ability. Sen. John McCain encouraged Graham to run, while Sen. Marco Rubio declined to make a decision.

Cable TV is facing a significant challenge as HBO announces plans to launch a standalone online streaming service in 2015, potentially marking the end of traditional cable television. This move, which comes after years of cord-cutting and cord-shaving trends, could redefine how consumers access premium content. HBO's decision to offer its content directly to consumers via the internet is seen as a direct threat to cable providers, who have long relied on bundling services to maintain subscriber numbers. While cable companies like Comcast and Charter may see a gradual loss of subscribers, the overall impact is expected to be limited. The move could also benefit competitors like Netflix and Hulu, as it validates the growing popularity of online streaming services. However, Amazon, which recently struck a deal with HBO, is likely to be left behind as HBO's direct service becomes the primary way for consumers to access its content. First Lady Michelle Obama inadvertently referred to herself as a "busy single mother" during an interview with CBS, quickly correcting herself to clarify her marital status. She humorously noted that being married to the President can sometimes feel like being a single mother. Obama discussed the challenges of balancing a busy schedule, emphasizing the importance of time and energy for managing a household and working. This slip-up sparked internet buzz, highlighting the public's interest in the First Lady's personal life and the complexities of her role.

A family's curse of fatal familial insomnia, a rare genetic disorder causing insomnia that leads to death, has affected multiple generations. The disease, first documented in a Venetian family in the 18th century, has been passed down through the Webbs and Vallabh families. Symptoms include sweating, dilated pupils, and a persistent inability to sleep. Doctors have linked the condition to misshapen prion proteins in the thalamus, a brain structure crucial for sleep and wake cycles. Despite no known cure, family members have turned to scientific research, with one couple quitting their jobs to pursue Ph.D.s in biology and founding the Prion Alliance to develop treatments. Their hope is that understanding this rare disease could lead to breakthroughs for more common neurological disorders.

Police in Beijing announced the arrests of five suspects involved in a suicide car crash near Tiananmen Square, calling it a planned terrorist attack and identifying the attackers as members of a Muslim minority, specifically Uighurs. The suspects were detained the same day as the Monday noon attack, 10 hours after it occurred. The SUV, driven by Usmen Hasan, contained gasoline, knives, and a flag with religious slogans. Two tourists, including a Filipino woman, were killed, and at least 38 people were injured. The five suspects, all with Uighur names, were caught with jihadi flags and knives in their temporary lodgings. The incident, Beijing's first known terrorist attack, has heightened security in Xinjiang, the Uighurs' home region. Critics warn that the government may use the attack to further repress Uighurs, citing past accusations without evidence.

The Bachelor's finale took an unexpected turn when Arie Luyendyk Jr. proposed to Becca Kufrin, only to change his mind and pursue Lauren Burnham, causing a public breakup. This unconventional move boosted ratings, drawing 7.8 million viewers. The episode's unedited split-screen footage of Arie and Becca's emotional breakdowns highlighted the producers' decision to maximize viewer engagement, despite the ethical concerns. Becca, while initially hurt, expressed a desire to move on and focus on her future. She was confirmed as the next Bachelorette, with her journey set to begin later in the year.

The brownstone that served as Carrie Bradshaw's home in "Sex and the City" is back on the market for $9.65 million, up from its previous sale price of $9 million. Located at 64 Perry St. in the West Village, the four-story, 4,100-square-foot home was the original setting for early episodes of the show but later switched to the next-door property at 66 Perry St. for the character's home. Now, potential buyers must contend with the constant presence of tourists, who flock to the address for its fame. The brownstone, listed with Sotheby’s International Realty, is currently available for showings.

America faces a significant challenge in scientific literacy, as evidenced by a recent National Science Foundation (NSF) poll. One in four Americans incorrectly believes the Earth revolves around the Sun, and a majority think astrology is a science. While the U.S. public generally supports science and its funding, only 6.5 out of 10 correct answers on a quiz about physical and biological sciences indicate a lack of basic understanding. The poll also highlights that schools are under pressure to teach creationism alongside evolution, undermining decades of scientific knowledge. This scientific illiteracy poses a threat to a nation that prides itself on scientific advancement, potentially leading to a second-rate education for children and the adoption of pseudo-scientific religious agendas.

Actor Douglas Rain, best known for voicing the AI computer HAL 9000 in the 1968 sci-fi film 2001: A Space Odyssey, has passed away at the age of 90. His chilling, dry voice became iconic, though he wasn't the first choice for the role. Director Stanley Kubrick selected Rain after hearing his voice in a 1960 documentary. Rain recorded all his lines in just 10 hours over two days, with Kubrick providing detailed explanations. Beyond HAL, Rain was an accomplished stage and screen actor, earning a Tony nomination for his role in Vivat! Vivat! Regina! on Broadway. His voice continues to evoke the complex and unsettling nature of artificial intelligence, influencing performances and technology in the decades since the film's release.

Residents in California's far northern counties, long feeling ignored and out of sync with urban areas, are considering forming their own state, Jefferson. Voters in Del Norte and Tehama counties will decide June 3 on an advisory measure to join this movement. Supporters argue for better representation and use of local resources, while opponents fear economic consequences. Similar efforts, including a proposal by Tim Draper to split California into six states, highlight ongoing dissatisfaction with state governance. However, such separations require approval from both state and federal legislatures, making the process challenging.

In western New York's upcoming special election, Democrat Kathy Hochul faces a narrow margin against Republican Jane Corwin. The race has shifted focus to Medicare, with Corwin defending the program and Hochul accused of wanting to cut it. Despite a $1.2 million investment from Republicans, Corwin trails and faces challenges from a Tea Party-backed candidate. The election is seen as crucial for Republicans, who are optimistic but acknowledge potential pitfalls.

Hurricane Harvey's aftermath has given rise to a new threat: a surge in mosquito populations, raising concerns about potential outbreaks of mosquito-borne diseases. Public health officials warn that the floodwater mosquitoes, which hatch from dormant eggs in standing water, could spread viruses like Zika, dengue, or West Nile. While most of these mosquitoes are considered nuisance species, their sheer numbers and aggressive biting behavior pose significant discomfort. Texas has launched aerial spraying campaigns to control the mosquito population and prevent disease outbreaks. Despite the current threat being more of a nuisance than a health hazard, the risk of West Nile and Zika returning is real, with the potential for increased cases in the coming months. Texans are advised to eliminate standing water, use mosquito repellent, and wear protective clothing to mitigate the risk.

- Ted Cruz issuing a public apology to Ben Carson for misleading reports about his campaign.

Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh faced new allegations of misconduct during a Senate Judiciary Committee interview, as investigators asked him about two previously undisclosed accusations. One claim, from an anonymous letter sent to Senator Cory Gardner, alleged Kavanaugh shoved a woman against a wall aggressively in 1998. Kavanaugh denied the allegation, calling it "ridiculous." A second claim, involving a man in Rhode Island, was recanted after being publicized. Kavanaugh also denied this allegation. These new claims come amid ongoing scrutiny of Kavanaugh, who has been accused by three other women. Senate Republicans are pushing for a confirmation vote, despite pressure from President Trump and some undecided GOP senators. Democrats are calling for more investigation and are concerned about the handling of anonymous allegations.

China has announced a ban on all ivory trade and processing activities by the end of 2017, a move that could significantly impact the global ivory market and help curb elephant poaching in Africa. The decision, hailed as a "game-changer" by conservation groups, follows years of international pressure and comes after China backed a Cites resolution in October. With China being the world's largest ivory market, accounting for an estimated 70% of global demand, the ban is expected to have a profound effect on elephant conservation efforts. The commercial processing and sale of ivory will cease by March 2017, with all registered traders phased out by the end of the year, marking a significant step towards protecting elephant populations from poaching.

A tiger killed a man and wounded another in Tbilisi after escaping from a zoo during severe flooding. The escaped tiger, found hiding in a disused warehouse, was shot dead by police who could not sedate it due to its aggressive behavior. The zoo had been overwhelmed by floodwaters, leading to the release of multiple animals, including lions, bears, and wolves, which roamed the streets. While the majority of animals drowned or were euthanized, the incident highlights the challenges zoos face during natural disasters.

Protesters toppled the controversial "Silent Sam" statue on the University of North Carolina Chapel Hill campus in Chapel Hill, N.C., on Monday, August 20, 2018. More than 300 people gathered at Peace and Justice Plaza, marched to the statue's base, and called for its removal. By 9:30 p.m., the statue was down. Tensions between police and protesters led to one arrest. Students, faculty, and alumni have long called for the statue's removal due to its racist image. The statue, given by the United Daughters of the Confederacy in 1909 and erected in 1913, was later moved by protesters using a rope, with some throwing dirt on it. Chapel Hill Police closed Franklin Street and formed a human barrier around the fallen monument. The University of North Carolina stated that the actions were dangerous but fortunate that no one was injured, and they are investigating the vandalism

A tapeworm found in fish from Asia has now been discovered in Alaskan salmon, raising concerns about the potential risks of consuming raw or undercooked fish. The Japanese broad tapeworm, Diphyllobothrium nihonkaiense, was identified in wild pink salmon from Alaska, prompting the Centers for Disease Control to warn that salmon from the American and Asian Pacific coasts and elsewhere pose potential dangers for those who eat these fish raw. While commercial sushi and ceviche should be safe due to FDA standards requiring frozen fish to kill parasites, consumers who catch or buy fresh salmon should freeze it first to destroy the tapeworm. Symptoms of tapeworm infection are often minor, but can include abdominal pain, nausea, loose stools, and weight loss. Effective treatment is available once the tapeworm is identified. The study highlights the need for increased awareness and vigilance regarding tapeworm infections, especially as global trade and consumption patterns change.

The Duchess of Cambridge may have inadvertently hinted at the gender of her baby during a recent visit. During a public appearance in Grimsby, England, Kate reportedly said, "Thank you, I’ll take that for my d..." before breaking off her sentence. A well-wisher suggested she was about to say "daughter," but Kate insisted they were not revealing the gender. Kate also mentioned her baby had been kicking "very much" and joked she might have to wait a long time before becoming queen. This exchange has sparked speculation in the media about the baby's gender, though St. James’s Palace confirmed the royal couple does not know and will not reveal the sex of their expected July baby.

Shuttle Atlantis undocked from the International Space Station on Sunday, marking its final voyage. The two crews bid farewell, with station commander Oleg Kotov urging Atlantis to "stay safe." Atlantis' crew will conduct a final safety inspection before landing on Wednesday. The station, now 98% complete, received new batteries and a Russian compartment. NASA plans two more shuttle missions to finish construction, with Atlantis possibly making one last trip in June 2011 for supplies. After retiring, Atlantis will be displayed in a museum, with the Smithsonian Institution set to receive Discovery. Atlantis' astronauts hope to park the shuttle in Houston, while the station's residents prepare for their return to Earth.

A 25-year-old Kentucky man, Michael Kerr, was banned from flying after attacking a flight crew on a Charlotte-bound American Airlines flight. Kerr, who had consumed three Jack Daniel's on board, refused to sit down after the plane had landed at Charlotte Douglas International Airport. He threatened to break the flight attendant's jaw and shoved her to the floor. The pilot and co-pilot subdued him, and he was later arrested. Kerr faces charges of being intoxicated and disruptive, assault on a female, communicating threats, and interfering with the duties of a flight crew or attendant. He was released on $25,000 bond and is banned from flying and contacting the flight attendant. The incident has raised concerns about the impact of alcohol on air travel and the safety of flight crews.

A study based on data from over a million U.S. teenagers spanning 24 years indicates that the legalization of medical marijuana does not lead to an increase in teen marijuana use. In states with medical marijuana laws, 16% of teens reported using marijuana in the past month, compared to 13% in states without such laws. Notably, in the 21 states that had medical marijuana laws by 2014, there was no significant change in teen marijuana use after the laws were enacted. The findings suggest that concerns about increased adolescent use due to medical marijuana laws may be unfounded. However, the study highlights the need to identify other factors influencing teen marijuana use.

U.S. Congressman Ralph Hall, 91, is hospitalized after a car accident in Fannin County, Texas, on Saturday afternoon. Hall, a passenger in a vehicle, was injured when it collided with another car on State Highway 121 near Trenton. He was airlifted to Medical Center of Plano in serious condition but has since been upgraded to stable condition. Hall suffered a hip injury and minor cuts and bruises but is expected to recover fully. The driver of the other vehicle was not injured. The accident is under investigation. Hall, the oldest serving member of Congress, was returning from the Fannin County Fair Parade in Bonham. He is scheduled to leave office in January after 17 consecutive terms.

The vice presidential candidates, Mike Pence and Tim Kaine, clashed over a range of issues during their debate, including tax returns, immigration, and foreign policy. Pence defended Donald Trump's tax avoidance strategies, while Kaine criticized Trump for not releasing his returns. They also debated the role of the U.S. in the world, with Kaine arguing for a more active approach and Pence supporting a focus on border security. Personal attacks and accusations of untrustworthiness were common, as both sides sought to undermine the other’s credibility. The debate highlighted the stark differences between the two teams and their visions for the country.

Martin Shkreli, convicted of securities fraud, was sentenced to seven years in prison, less than half of the government's request but more than the defense's plea. Shkreli, known for raising the price of a life-saving drug by 5,000 percent, apologized for his actions and admitted fault. He faces a $75,000 fine and must forfeit $7.3 million. His defense highlighted his intelligence and potential, while prosecutors emphasized his fraud and lack of respect for the law. Shkreli's behavior during the trial, including offering money for a strand of Hillary Clinton's hair, contributed to his harsher sentence.

A father heard terrified screams from his daughter's kidnappers on Thursday evening and learned she was missing, but a ransom call the next day ended without a proof of life. Police launched a large-scale search involving about 1,200 officers. Two suspects, a 39-year-old and a 61-year-old, were arrested after their cell phones were tracked and DNA evidence matched one of them. The father, a well-known businessman, was reportedly offered a million euros ransom. His daughter, 17, was found dead in an abandoned farmyard near their home. Both parents are receiving psychological support from police.

Researchers have uncovered a series of mass graves in south Texas, containing the bodies of unidentified migrants. In the Sacred Heart Burial Park in Falfurrias, anthropologists found multiple individuals stuffed into garbage, shopping, and body bags, dumped into crowded graves. The discovery was made by professors and students from the University of Indianapolis and Baylor University, working on a project to identify undocumented migrants who died while crossing the border. In 2013, they exhumed 110 corpses, and in a recent excavation, found 52 plots with remains. The bodies were buried by a local funeral home since 2005, with Brooks County officials paying $450 for each migrant body. The remains were found in various states of decomposition, with some bones in biohazard bags between coffins. The discovery highlights the issue of unidentified migrants and the inadequate handling of their remains, raising ethical concerns.

You don't need to take "literally" literally anymore: The Oxford English Dictionary has officially updated the definition of the word to include its common, non-literal usage. Initially defined as "in a literal way or sense," the dictionary now notes that "literally" can also be used for emphasis rather than being actually true, such as "we were literally killing ourselves laughing." This change, added in the September 2011 edition but unnoticed until recently, offers relief to those who have been ridiculed for using the term incorrectly. Senior editor Fiona McPherson humorously noted that it "seems to have literally slipped under the radar."

The "Remain" and "Leave" camps in the UK's EU referendum are evenly matched, with Prime Minister David Cameron leading the "Remain" effort, supported by most major political parties and businesses. The "Leave" campaign, spearheaded by Michael Gove and Boris Johnson, focuses on sovereignty and immigration. The possibility of Brexit is causing global market concerns, with stocks and the pound falling as the June 23 referendum approaches. Polls suggest momentum is shifting towards "Leave," but experts caution that the final outcome is uncertain. The "Remain" side warns of economic recession, while "Leave" promises control over spending and reduced immigration. The outcome remains uncertain as the campaign enters its final days.

The discovery of a model of George W. Bush's impaled head in Game of Thrones season one, revealed in a Reddit post and acknowledged by show creators David Benioff and D.B. Weiss in a DVD commentary, has led to apologies from HBO. The producers state they meant no disrespect and will remove the head from future DVD productions. HBO expresses dismay and finds the inclusion unacceptable, disrespectful, and in very bad taste.

A 46-year-old woman from Seneca Falls, NY, was arrested for driving under the influence after consuming two bottles of pure vanilla extract, which has an alcohol content similar to vodka or gin. Carolyn Kesel, who had a prior DWI conviction in 2006, was found driving erratically in the Macedon Walmart parking lot. Her blood alcohol content was .26%, more than three times the legal limit. Police are now aware of the high alcohol content in common food extracts and are concerned about the potential for habitual alcoholics to use these as a masking tool.

The United States and Israel have announced their withdrawal from UNESCO, citing anti-Israel bias and the need for "fundamental reform" within the organization. The U.S. stopped funding UNESCO in 2011 after the agency admitted Palestine as a full member. The U.S. will maintain its presence as an observer state. The decision, effective as of December 31, 2018, is seen as a major blow to UNESCO, which relies on U.S. funding for about 22% of its budget. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson made the decision, citing concerns over mounting arrears and anti-Israel bias. UNESCO Director-General Irina Bokova expressed disappointment, calling it a loss for multilateralism and the United Nations family. The U.S. move is part of a broader trend of the U.S. withdrawing from international organizations, including the Paris climate accord and the U.N. Human Rights Council.

A 7-year-old boy named Yamato Tanooka was found alive after going missing for six days in a forest in Hokkaido, Japan. Yamato was discovered by military personnel in a hut on an exercise area, about 5 kilometers from where he was last seen. His parents initially told police that he had gone missing while they were out collecting wild vegetables, but later admitted they had left him as punishment for throwing stones at people and cars. Yamato, who was found dehydrated but otherwise healthy, was reunited with his family and his father apologized, stating, "I really didn't think it would come to that. We went too far." The case sparked a national debate about parental discipline.

Elderly South Koreans reunited with long-lost relatives in North Korea after a six-decade separation, marking a rare show of cooperation between the two Koreas. The six-day family reunion, approved after a three-year hiatus, brought together 82 participants, chosen by lottery from over 70,000 applicants. The average age of the participants is 84, many arriving with canes or in wheelchairs. Emotional scenes included frail participants entering the ballroom on stretchers, and families sharing photos and stories. The reunions, held at Mount Kumgang, are brief and occur only a few times a year, with North Korea's approval. The event, despite concerns over upcoming joint military exercises, signifies a shared interest in reconnecting long-separated families.

An investigation is ongoing in Washington County, Pennsylvania, after a man removed his monitoring bracelet, kidnapped his wife, and allegedly killed her in a remote area. Tierne Ewing, 48, was found dead in a barn with a gunshot wound to the head. Her estranged husband, Kevin Ewing, 47, was found alive with a self-inflicted gunshot wound, declared brain-dead at a hospital. Kevin Ewing had previously been accused of holding Tierne hostage for 12 days, beating and burning her. He was released on $100,000 bail after posting it, despite prosecutors' concerns. Kevin Ewing had removed the electronic monitoring bracelet before the alleged abduction. The couple was last seen in a gray Hyundai Veloster, found abandoned in a wooded area. Police found a .22-caliber firearm, sleeping bags, and other camping items in the barn. Kevin Ewing's parents' home was the location where Tierne was staying

2011 is proving to be a challenging year for the Favre family. Brett Favre, the former NFL quarterback, faces a sexual harassment lawsuit from former massage therapists, and his younger sister, Brandi Favre, was arrested in a meth lab raid. The meth lab was discovered in a condo complex in Diamondhead, Mississippi, where authorities found methamphetamine cooking in the bathtub. Brandi Favre, 34, is facing two felony counts and is scheduled to appear before a judge. The incident occurred less than 10 miles from where Brett Favre and his siblings grew up. Additionally, Brett Favre was fined $50,000 by the NFL for a 2008 incident involving inappropriate messages and pictures sent to a broadcaster.

Rowan County Clerk Kim Davis has filed a last-minute pleading with a federal judge, asking him not to hold her in contempt for refusing to issue marriage licenses. Davis argues that complying with the judge's August order to resume issuing licenses would violate her conscience due to her religious objections to same-sex marriage. She claims broad political support, with Kentucky legislators from both parties expressing a desire to accommodate her religious beliefs. The contempt hearing is set for Thursday. Meanwhile, Republican Senate President Robert Stivers has asked the judge to delay his ruling, arguing that the state legislature needs time to address the issue. Stivers and House Speaker Greg Stumbo favor a special legislative session but doubt it will occur due to Governor Steve Beshear's reluctance to call one. U.S. Attorney Kerry B. Harvey has expressed concerns about Davis's refusal to comply with the court's order.

Qatar Airways CEO Akbar Al Baker has apologized for suggesting that women are not capable of running the airline. At the International Air Transport Association's annual conference in Sydney, Al Baker stated that his position as airline CEO is "a very challenging position" and must be led by a man. His comments drew criticism and backlash. In a statement, Al Baker expressed his "heartfelt apologies" and defended Qatar Airways' record on gender equality, citing the airline's employment of female pilots and engineers. He also stated that he would be "pleased" to develop a female candidate to become the next CEO. Al Baker has faced criticism before for making controversial statements, including calling American flight attendants "grandmothers."

Georgia mother Leanna Harris, whose 22-month-old son Cooper died after being left in a hot SUV, has drawn scrutiny for her calm demeanor and statements to authorities. Prosecutors allege that Leanna, like her husband Ross, researched children dying in hot vehicles. During the probable cause hearing for Ross, Leanna's behavior was described as odd; she remained stoic when informed her son was missing and asked Ross if he had said too much to police. Despite not being charged, Leanna's role in the case is under investigation, with some legal experts suggesting she could face charges if Ross is convicted. Leanna maintains her loyalty to Ross, saying she loves him and is standing by him, even as details of Ross's sexting and research on child deaths in vehicles continue to emerge.

During an AFC Champions League match between Iran's Sepahan and Saudi Arabia's Al-Ahli, Sepahan midfielder Adel Kolahkaj picked up a piece of trash and threw it off the field—only to discover it was an explosive device that detonated. The incident, which occurred at Foolad Shahr Stadium, highlights the unexpected dangers players face during matches.

The author expresses gratitude to President Donald Trump, his son-in-law Jared Kushner, and others for their support and contributions in commuting the sentence of Ms. Alice Marie Johnson, describing it as an inspirational moment that brings hope to many deserving of a second chance.

A parolee suspected of cutting off his ankle monitor and carrying out a series of killings in the Houston area has been arrested and charged with capital murder. Jose Gilberto Rodriguez, 46, a high-risk registered sex offender, is accused of at least three slayings and two other violent robberies in the past week. Rodriguez was apprehended without incident after a nine-day manhunt, leading to relief among Harris County residents. The suspected serial killer, who had previously served time for attempted aggravated sexual assault and other offenses, is expected to face three capital murder charges. Houston Police Chief Art Acevedo promised to create a new task force to address the issue of parole violators.

Washington, D.C., is embarking on a three-year, $1.5 million project to estimate the city's entire cat population, both feral and pet cats, through the D.C. Cat Count. This initiative involves using camera traps, household surveys, and shelter analyses to gather data. The project aims to improve understanding and management of the city's cat population, addressing concerns about wildlife impact and pest control. By involving the community, the project hopes to gain support and participation, ultimately providing valuable insights into the dynamics of D.C.'s feline residents.

A 24-year-old woman named Laura, who has suffered from depression since childhood, has been granted the right to die by Belgian doctors, marking a small but growing trend of younger individuals seeking euthanasia. Laura, who entered a psychiatric facility at 21, told local newspaper De Morgen that life is not for her, expressing that death feels not like a choice but a necessity. She plans her funeral and final words to her mother and grandmother, attributing her suffering to both her upbringing and an inherent death wish. The date of her death is yet to be decided, as the case highlights an increase in requests for euthanasia from non-terminal patients. Belgium legalized euthanasia in 2002, with about 1,400 cases annually, and in 2013, the law was expanded to include terminally ill children.

In Super Bowl XLIX, the University of Phoenix Stadium witnessed both a memorable catch and an unconventional celebration. Seattle Seahawks receiver Jermaine Kearse made a remarkable catch late in the fourth quarter, staying on the ground long enough for the ball to bounce up, allowing him to secure the touchdown that gave the Seahawks a 10-point lead. However, the celebration turned controversial when Seahawks wide receiver Doug Baldwin appeared to defecate on the football after scoring, drawing a 15-yard penalty. Despite the incident, the play was crucial in giving Seattle the lead, only for the Patriots to eventually win the game 28-24, with New England cornerback Malcolm Butler making a game-sealing interception.

Passengers and crew on a Tianjin Airlines flight in China's Xinjiang region thwarted a hijacking attempt by six people shortly after takeoff. The plane, which had just departed from Hotan for Urumqi, returned to Hotan airport where the suspects were detained, according to a regional government news portal. The Tianshan regional government's news portal reported that at least seven passengers and crew were injured in the incident, but did not provide further details about the hijackers' motives or identities. The attempt occurred in a region with a history of tensions between the Uighur minority and Han Chinese, and the government has invested in the region to raise living standards amid concerns over organized terrorist threats.

ABC's shows will be available on Apple's iPad through a new app, the ABC Player, allowing viewers to watch free, ad-supported episodes from 20 ABC shows via Wi-Fi and purchase episodes via iTunes. The announcement comes as ABC's "Modern Family" featured the iPad in a recent episode. Apple CEO Steve Jobs is a board director of the network.

Groupon is reportedly about to close a $950 million funding round, potentially valuing the company between $4 billion and $8 billion. This move comes after Groupon CEO Andrew Mason rejected Google's $6 billion offer, indicating Groupon's ambition for global domination. To achieve this, Groupon is likely to rapidly acquire rival group-buying companies, expand its local sales force, and make significant technology investments. While much of the funding will be used to cash out existing investors, Groupon's substantial capital will enable it to solidify its market position and potentially change e-commerce.

Longtime conservative columnist George Will has left the Republican Party and is urging others to ensure Donald Trump does not win the nomination. "Make sure he loses," Will told PJ Media, adding that this is not his party anymore. Will, a Pulitzer Prize-winning columnist, has long criticized Trump, warning that he would be the "most unpopular nominee ever" and unable to garner support from women, minorities, and young voters. His voter registration in Maryland has changed from Republican to "unaffiliated." Will's decision comes after House Speaker Paul Ryan endorsed Trump.

A shooting at the Eaton Centre in Toronto left one man dead and seven others injured, including a 13-year-old boy in critical condition. Multiple people were hit by bullets or injured in the chaos as shoppers fled. The suspect, described as a black man with dreadlocks, fled the scene. Police are reviewing mall security footage and interviewing witnesses. Mayor Rob Ford and Premier Dalton McGuinty offered condolences. The incident has raised concerns about safety in public spaces.

The TV One network launches "Find Our Missing," a docudrama aimed at addressing the underrepresentation of missing minorities in national media. The show, hosted by "Law & Order" actress S. Epatha Merkerson, focuses on two cases: the disappearance of Pamela Butler, a 47-year-old federal employee from Washington, D.C., and a 5-year-old boy named Hasanni Campbell who vanished in Oakland, California. The series emphasizes the personal impact on families and encourages viewers to provide information. Despite the significant number of missing African-Americans, their cases rarely receive the same attention as those of other demographics. The show hopes to raise awareness and potentially aid in the resolution of these cases, highlighting the broader issue of racial disparities in missing-person coverage.

Portland police arrested over 50 people as they cleared encampments of the Occupy movement, part of a nationwide trend of authorities shutting down similar protests. The Portland authorities issued an eviction notice and then moved to empty the camps and fence them off. While many protesters left on their own, others chose to stay, leading to a standoff with police in riot gear. The confrontation continued into late afternoon, with protesters chanting and police warning of potential use of chemical agents and impact weapons. Demonstrators regrouped in the streets, blocking traffic for hours. In other cities, similar actions were taken, with officials citing health and safety issues as the basis for their actions. The Occupy movement faced increased pressure as officials in various cities warned of potential confrontations and arrests.

The 60 Minutes interview with Stormy Daniels, an adult-film star who claims she had an affair with Donald Trump, will air on Sunday, March 25 at 7 p.m. ET/PT on CBS. Daniels will discuss the relationship she says she had with Trump in 2006 and 2007, revealing details that bring her story up to the present. The president has denied the affair. The segment will also examine the potential legal and political ramifications of the $130,000 payment made by Trump's attorney, Michael Cohen, to Daniels. Daniels is seeking a ruling that the confidentiality agreement between her and Trump is invalid, in part because Trump never signed it. Trump's attorneys are seeking to move the case to federal court and claim Daniels is liable for more than $20 million in damages for violations of the agreement.

Egypt's security forces clashed with protesters in Tahrir Square early Saturday, resulting in at least two deaths and dozens wounded. The military attempted to disperse the peaceful demonstrators, contradicting its own claims of no fatalities. Protest leaders issued statements aimed at de-escalating tensions. Despite the military's efforts, thousands remained in the square, setting up tents and challenging the military's tactics. The incident highlights ongoing frustrations with the military's rule and the need for democratic changes.

Martha Kunkle, who died in 1995, has become an infamous example of the widespread and problematic practice of robo-signing in the debt-collection industry. Her name appeared on thousands of affidavits submitted by Portfolio Recovery Associates Inc. to sue borrowers for credit-card debts. After being sued for fraud, the company stopped using Kunkle's name in affidavits in early 2008. However, in July 2008, Kunkle's name was used again in a lawsuit against a Seattle woman, raising concerns about the accuracy and reliability of documentation in debt collection. The case highlights the issue of mass-produced, sloppy, and inaccurate affidavits in the industry. Minnesota's attorney general is investigating numerous buyers and collectors of consumer debt for falsifying affidavits, while some judges and regulators argue that the use of Kunkle's name reflects an epidemic of such practices. Tucson police are holding a Colt Thompson submachine gun confiscated from John Dillinger during his 1934 capture. Peru, Indiana, claims the weapon was stolen from their police station in 1933 by one of Dillinger’s accomplices posing as an insurance agent. Peru officials believe the gun’s serial number can prove their case. Tucson police see the weapon as a significant part of their city’s history but acknowledge it’s challenging to determine the weapon’s origin. The dispute highlights the historical significance of the gun in both Tucson and Peru.

Arkansas fired football coach Bobby Petrino on Tuesday, citing his "knowingly misleading" behavior regarding his relationship with his mistress, Jessica Dorrell. Athletic director Jeff Long announced Petrino's termination, alleging Petrino had ignored multiple chances to come clean about the relationship, which Long called "workplace favoritism." Petrino, who hired Dorrell as student-athlete development coordinator and gave her $20,000, was also accused of intentionally misleading Long and the public about her presence at his motorcycle accident. Long stated Petrino abused his authority by hiring Dorrell and jeopardizing the football program's integrity. Petrino, who led Arkansas to a 34-17 record in four seasons, issued an apology, focusing on healing his family.

A man in Madison County, Illinois, is suing Pepsi for finding a mouse in his Mountain Dew, claiming the soda made him violently ill. Pepsi's defense? The mouse would have dissolved in the soda before consumption, leaving no trace. The lawsuit, filed in Madison County Circuit Court, alleges that Pepsi failed to adequately prepare, inspect, and package its product, causing injuries, medical bills, disability, lost wages, and pain and suffering. PepsiCo and Supervalu, which supplied the vending machine, are named as defendants. The case seeks at least $50,000 in damages.

An Australian man named Gable Tostee, 30, has been acquitted of murder and manslaughter charges related to the death of Warriena Wright, 26, during their first Tinder date. Tostee and Wright met on the dating app and had a brief encounter at a Gold Coast resort before Wright fell to her death from his 14th-floor balcony. Prosecutors argued Tostee intimidated Wright and forced her onto the balcony, while his defense highlighted a 199-minute audio recording on his phone showing Tostee pleading with Wright to stay and offering to make her a meal. After a four-day trial, the jury found Tostee not guilty. Tostee expressed relief and said he was looking forward to moving on with his life.

In his closing arguments, Pistorius' lawyer Barry Roux portrayed the athlete as a vulnerable man suffering from years of insecurity due to his disability, comparing his anxiety to that of an abused woman. Roux suggested that Pistorius, feeling vulnerable and anxious, accidentally shot his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp when he mistook her for an intruder. The defense maintained that Pistorius did not intentionally kill Steenkamp. Roux admitted that Pistorius had been argumentative as a witness but argued that the athlete was guilty of negligence for discharging a gun in a crowded restaurant. The judge is expected to announce a verdict soon.

Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton won the South Carolina primary, defeating Bernie Sanders with 74% of the vote, as African-American voters, who made up 61% of the electorate, strongly supported her. Clinton's victory, which included 87% of black voters, marked a significant shift from 2008 when Barack Obama won 78% of black votes. Clinton's campaign focused on economic issues, and her husband Bill Clinton's presence bolstered her appeal. Sanders, despite losing, plans to continue his campaign, particularly targeting states with large minority populations. The win positions Clinton strongly for Super Tuesday, where she aims to secure a delegate lead.

A New Year's Eve stampede in Shanghai's Bund area killed at least 36 people and injured 47, according to Chinese President Xi Jinping's demand for an investigation. The crush began just before midnight in Chenyi Square, where large crowds had gathered for the countdown. Despite the cancellation of New Year's Day festivities, the crowd size was similar to the previous year, with close to 300,000 people expected. Police regretted their failure to intervene in time, with fewer officers deployed than for some other events. The cause of the stampede remains under investigation, with some reports suggesting it was triggered by people rushing to pick up fake money thrown from a building. The incident has sparked criticism of authorities for inadequate crowd control measures.

Saturday Night Live began their latest episode with a message of support to Paris after the recent terrorist attacks, skipping their usual cold open. Cecily Strong, a cast member, delivered a powerful statement: "Paris is the city of light, and here in New York City, we know that light will never go out. Our love and support is with everyone there tonight. We stand with you." She repeated the message in French.

Actor Bryan Cranston hinted during an interview with CNN that a comeback for the hit AMC series Breaking Bad isn't completely off the table. When asked about the fate of his character Walter White, a.k.a. Heisenberg, following the show's series finale, Cranston responded cryptically, "You never saw bags zip up or anyone say... you know." This enigmatic response has fans speculating about the possibility of Walter White's return. While the highly acclaimed series concluded in 2013, a spinoff series Better Call Saul is currently in production. Creator Vince Gilligan has also hinted at potential cameos from Breaking Bad characters in the upcoming series. For now, Breaking fans can hold onto their hazmat jumpsuits, as Cranston's teasing response leaves the fate of Walter White open to interpretation.

Apple's recent iOS 5.0.1 update, intended to fix battery drain issues, has left some iPhone users unsatisfied. Despite the update, many report their batteries are still draining rapidly, even under light usage. Some users experienced a 20% battery drain in just 45 minutes with Wi-Fi and location services on, while others noted a significant drop in battery life overnight. Apple has acknowledged some remaining issues but continues to investigate. Users are advised to perform a full reset or backup and restore to address the problem. The battery drain issue isn't new, having affected earlier iPhone models and iOS versions. However, the recent update hasn't resolved the problem for a significant number of users, indicating potential ongoing issues with iOS 5.0.1.

Police have made a breakthrough in the 47-year-old abduction of three-year-old Cheryl Grimmer from a Wollongong beach, urging a suspect who would now be in his 60s to come forward. Detectives believe they have identified a teenager, aged 17-18 at the time, after finding information missed in the original investigation. Cheryl's family, including her brothers, have appealed to the suspect for closure. The case remains unsolved, with the NSW government offering a $100,000 reward for information leading to an arrest. Cheryl's parents died without knowing what happened to their daughter.

A Texas high school cheerleader who was dismissed from her squad for refusing to cheer for a basketball player accused of sexually assaulting her lost an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. The Supreme Court declined to hear the case without comment. The cheerleader, identified by her initials H.S., was 16 when she claimed she was raped at a party in 2008. At a 2009 basketball game, H.S. refused to cheer for the player, leading to her removal from the squad. Federal courts ruled that the cheerleader acted as a "mouthpiece" for the school and had no First Amendment right to remain silent. The case garnered attention due to the sexual assault allegations and the cheerleader's refusal to support her attacker.

French scientists have developed a fully artificial, self-regulating heart that can beat for up to five years, offering a potential solution to the chronic shortage of donor hearts for transplant surgery. The device, created by the biomedical firm Carmat, was implanted in a 75-year-old Frenchman during a 10-hour operation. Unlike other artificial hearts, this one is completely artificial and self-regulating, mimicking the functions of a real heart with electrical sensors and microprocessors that monitor the body's demands for blood. The cost is estimated at £100,000 to £135,000, similar to the overall cost of a transplanted donor heart. The device, weighing 900g and designed to fit 86% of men, is being tested in four patients in France and is expected to be available for wider use by early 2015.
